subject: do

questions.question: Give example of a linear integer minimization problem (LIP), and define the following (i) the relaxed problem of the LIP, (ii) an upper bound of the original LIP problem. [2 + 2 + 2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Example LIP:
$$\min\ 5x_1 + 3x_2 \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x_1 + x_2 \ge 2,\quad x_1, x_2 \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$$
(i) Relaxed problem: drop the integer requirement and keep only the bounds, so the variables become real:
$$\min\ 5x_1 + 3x_2 \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x_1 + x_2 \ge 2,\quad 0 \le x_1, x_2 \le 3$$
Its feasible set contains every feasible point of the LIP, so its optimal value is a lower bound on the LIP optimum (here the LP optimum is $x = (0, 2)$ with value 6).
(ii) Upper bound: the objective value of any (integer) feasible solution of the original LIP. For example $(x_1, x_2) = (2, 2)$ is feasible ($2 + 2 = 4 \ge 2$) and gives $5(2) + 3(2) = 16$, so $16 \ge \text{OPT}$. In branch and bound the best feasible solution found so far (the incumbent) is the upper bound and it is lowered whenever a better feasible solution is found.

rubric.point: A correct linear integer minimisation problem: linear objective, linear constraint(s), integer variables
Relaxed problem: same objective and constraints with the integrality replaced by continuous bounds (its value is a lower bound)
Upper bound: the objective value of any feasible integer solution of the original problem, with an example value

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf p. 1 (same example; the values 6 and 16 are added here). Course notes: relaxation and bounds in DisCopt.pdf PDF pp. 46–48 (sections 3.2–3.2.2). For a minimisation: relaxation → lower bound, feasible solution → upper bound.

questions.question: Given a set of items $S = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}$ and $m$ proper subsets $S_j$ of $S$, $j = 1, 2, \cdots, m$. You wants to covers all items in $S$ by choosing a number of $S_j$ with minimum cost; the cost of choosing $S_j$ is $c_j$. Write down the mathematical model of the weighted set covering problem by defining decision variables for optimization. Describe the physical meaning of the constraint sets in the mathematical model. [3+1 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Data: $a_{ij} = 1$ if item $i$ is in $S_j$, $a_{ij} = 0$ otherwise ($i = 1, \dots, n$; $j = 1, \dots, m$).
Decision variables: $x_j = 1$ if subset $S_j$ is chosen, $x_j = 0$ otherwise.
$$\min \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j x_j$$
$$\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^{m} a_{ij} x_j \ge 1, \quad i = 1, \dots, n$$
$$x_j \in \{0, 1\}, \quad j = 1, \dots, m$$
Meaning: the objective is the total cost of the chosen subsets. The constraint for item $i$ says that at least one chosen subset contains item $i$, i.e. every item of $S$ is covered at least once. $x_j \in \{0, 1\}$: each subset is either taken or not.

rubric.point: Defines $x_j$ (1 if $S_j$ chosen, else 0) and the incidence data $a_{ij}$
Objective $\min \sum_j c_j x_j$
Covering constraints $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \ge 1$ for every item $i$, with $x_j \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning: every item must be covered by at least one chosen subset

questions.question:
Consider the following bi-partite graph
for which the costs $c_{ij}$ are given as
$$c_{11} = 2, c_{12} = 3, c_{13} = 4,$$
$$c_{21} = 3, c_{22} = 4, c_{23} = 1,$$
$$c_{31} = 4, c_{32} = 2, c_{33} = 3.$$
Define the variables for the minimization problem and present your mathematical model. Define the meaning of each of your 6 constraints involved. [3 + 2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Variables: $x_{ij} = 1$ if worker $i$ is assigned to job $j$, $x_{ij} = 0$ otherwise ($i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$).
$$\min \sum_{i=1}^{3}\sum_{j=1}^{3} c_{ij}x_{ij} = 2x_{11} + 3x_{12} + 4x_{13} + 3x_{21} + 4x_{22} + x_{23} + 4x_{31} + 2x_{32} + 3x_{33}$$
subject to the 6 constraints
$$x_{11} + x_{12} + x_{13} = 1,\quad x_{21} + x_{22} + x_{23} = 1,\quad x_{31} + x_{32} + x_{33} = 1$$
$$x_{11} + x_{21} + x_{31} = 1,\quad x_{12} + x_{22} + x_{32} = 1,\quad x_{13} + x_{23} + x_{33} = 1$$
$$x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$$
Meaning: the first three (one per worker, $\sum_j x_{ij} = 1$) say each worker $i$ does exactly one job; the last three (one per job, $\sum_i x_{ij} = 1$) say each job $j$ is done by exactly one worker.
(Not asked, but useful: the optimum is $x_{11} = x_{23} = x_{32} = 1$ with cost $2 + 1 + 2 = 5$; checking all $3! = 6$ assignments gives 9, 5, 9, 8, 9, 12.)

rubric.point: Binary variables $x_{ij}$ defined (worker $i$ to job $j$)
Objective $\min \sum_i \sum_j c_{ij} x_{ij}$ with the given costs
All 6 assignment constraints written, plus $x_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$
Meaning of the 3 worker constraints: each worker gets exactly one job
Meaning of the 3 job constraints: each job gets exactly one worker

questions.question: Define an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm of a minimization problem in combinatorial optimization. [2 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $P$ be a minimisation problem with set of instances $\mathcal{I}$, and let $A$ be an algorithm that returns a feasible solution $A(I)$ for every instance $I \in \mathcal{I}$. $A$ is an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm ($\alpha \ge 1$) if it runs in polynomial time and
$$A(I) \le \alpha \cdot OPT(I) \quad \text{for all } I \in \mathcal{I},$$
where $OPT(I)$ is the optimal value of instance $I$. So the solution is never worse than $\alpha$ times the optimum (e.g. Christofides for the metric STSP has $\alpha = 3/2$).

rubric.point: Feasible solution for every instance found in polynomial time
$A(I) \le \alpha\, OPT(I)$ for all instances, with $\alpha \ge 1$

questions.question: State one of the most important properties of the MST (minimum spanning tree) subgraph of a graph. Find the MST sub-graph by inspection of the undirected graph below in Fig. 1, where the distance or cost of various edges are $c_{12} = c_{13} = c_{24} = c_{34} = 1$, $c_{14} = 2$ and $c_{23} = 3$ [1 + 3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
Property: the MST is a tree, so it connects all the vertices with no cycles (hence exactly $n - 1$ edges), and it has the minimum possible total edge weight of all spanning trees.
MST by inspection: there are 4 vertices, so the tree needs $4 - 1 = 3$ edges. The four edges of cost 1 form the cycle 1–2–4–3–1; any three of them connect all four vertices without a cycle. Take
$$T = \{(1,2), (1,3), (2,4)\}, \qquad \text{cost} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.$$
It is minimum because every spanning tree has 3 edges and every edge costs at least 1, so no tree can cost less than 3. The diagonals $(1,4)$ (cost 2) and $(2,3)$ (cost 3) are not used. (Kruskal gives the same: take the unit edges in turn and skip the one that would close the cycle.) Any other choice of three unit edges is an equally good MST.

rubric.point: One correct property: spans/connects all vertices, no cycles ($n-1$ edges), minimum total weight
Three edges of cost 1 chosen that connect all 4 vertices without a cycle
Total cost 3 stated, with a reason it is minimal (or that the diagonals are not used)

questions.question: Explain why there are $(n-1)!$ possible distinct routes (solutions) in a Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (ATSP) with $n$ cities. How many solutions are there in the quadratic assignment problem with $n$ facilities and $n$ locations? Why? [2 + 3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
ATSP: a tour is a cyclic order of the $n$ cities, so fix the home (starting) city; it does not matter where the cycle starts. The second city can then be any of the remaining $n-1$ cities, the third any of the remaining $n-2$, …, the last is forced. So there are
$$1 \times (n-1)(n-2)\cdots 2 \times 1 = (n-1)!$$
distinct routes. In the ATSP $c_{ij} \ne c_{ji}$ in general, so a tour and its reverse are different routes with different lengths and both are counted. (For the symmetric TSP a tour and its reverse have the same length, which gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(n-1)!$.)
QAP: there are $n!$ solutions. A solution is a one-to-one assignment of the $n$ facilities to the $n$ locations, i.e. a permutation $\phi \in S_n$: facility 1 can go to any of $n$ locations, facility 2 to any of the remaining $n-1$, …, facility $n$ to the last one, giving $n(n-1)\cdots 1 = n!$. Unlike a tour there is no rotation to factor out, because every location is a distinct place.

rubric.point: Fix the starting city: the remaining $n-1$ cities can be ordered in $(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1$ ways
Asymmetric: a tour and its reverse are different, so all $(n-1)!$ count
QAP has $n!$ solutions
Reason: each solution is a permutation (one-to-one assignment) of $n$ facilities to $n$ locations: $n(n-1)\cdots 1$

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf p. 4. Course notes: tour counts, DisCopt.pdf PDF p. 21 ("(n − 1)! possible tours … in the asymmetric TSP (and ½(n − 1)! for the symmetric TSP with home city being fixed)"); QAP as a permutation problem, PDF pp. 33–34 (eq. 69).
questions.keyDispute: The handwritten solution adds "for any tour, regardless of STSP or ATSP, the reverse way of travelling will result in the same distance, hence (n−1)!/2". That only holds for the symmetric TSP; for the ATSP asked here the answer is (n−1)!, as the notes (PDF p. 21) say.

questions.question:
Consider the 7 city symmetric TSP with a feasible tour $x = (1, 3, 2, 6, 7, 4, 5)$ where the 1st city is the starting city. Answer the following questions:
Construct two 2-Opt neighbors of $x$. Construct an example of a sub-tour that may occur in the solution process. [2 + 3 Marks ]
questions.modelAnswer:
2-opt move: delete the edges $(c_i, c_{i+1})$ and $(c_j, c_{j+1})$, add $(c_i, c_j)$ and $(c_{i+1}, c_{j+1})$, which reverses positions $i+1, \dots, j$. Positions (not city labels) of $x$: $c_1 = 1, c_2 = 3, c_3 = 2, c_4 = 6, c_5 = 7, c_6 = 4, c_7 = 5$.
• $i = 1, j = 3$: remove (1,3) and (2,6), add (1,2) and (3,6), reverse "3, 2" → $x^{(1)} = (1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 4, 5)$.
• $i = 1, j = 4$: remove (1,3) and (6,7), add (1,6) and (3,7), reverse "3, 2, 6" → $x^{(2)} = (1, 6, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5)$.
(Another: $i = 2, j = 4$ gives $(1, 3, 6, 2, 7, 4, 5)$.)
Sub-tour: if the subtour elimination constraints are left out, the degree constraints $\sum_{e \in \delta(i)} x_e = 2$ can be met by several separate cycles instead of one tour, e.g.
$$1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1 \quad\text{and}\quad 6 \to 7 \to 4 \to 5 \to 6.$$
Every city has degree 2, but the salesman never travels between $\{1, 2, 3\}$ and $\{4, 5, 6, 7\}$, so it is not a tour. In the STSP a sub-tour needs at least 3 cities (2 cities would need the same undirected edge twice). The constraint $\sum_{e \in E(S)} x_e \le |S| - 1$ for $S = \{1, 2, 3\}$ is violated (3 edges > 2), which is how such solutions are cut off.

rubric.point: First valid 2-opt neighbour (two edges removed, the segment between them reversed)
Second, different valid 2-opt neighbour
A sub-tour example on the 7 cities: two or more disjoint cycles covering all cities
Why it is a sub-tour / not a tour (each cycle has ≥ 3 cities in the STSP; violates $\sum_{e\in E(S)} x_e \le |S|-1$)

questions.explanation: Follows the handwritten solution in Past Paper Solutions 2024 Exam.pdf pp. 4–5 (neighbours 1236745 and 1623745; sub-tours drawn as two cycles). Course notes: the 2-opt move and the neighbour list for a 7-city tour, DisCopt.pdf PDF pp. 26–27; STSP model and subtour elimination constraints, PDF pp. 22–23.
